title: The iconostasis
hook: a wall of icons between the nave and the altar

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Liturgy: sung almost from start to finish, with earthly cares left at the door. Your line was heaven on earth. Did you hear the waves of Lord, have mercy? Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

From the back of a Byzantine church, the first thing you notice isn't the altar. You can barely see the altar. What you see is a wall. A screen of wood or stone, running the width of the church, covered in painted faces on gold. Saints. Angels. A mother and child. A man with a long beard holding a scroll. Their eyes look straight out at you. In the middle there are doors, and every so often, during the liturgy, the doors open, a deacon comes through with incense, and for a moment you glimpse the altar behind. Then the doors close, and the faces are watching again. Today's word is that wall.
screen: `A WALL OF PAINTED FACES.` → `DOORS IN THE MIDDLE.` → `THE ALTAR, GLIMPSED.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The iconostasis stands between the nave, where the people pray, and the sanctuary, where the altar is. It has a central pair of doors, called the Royal or Holy Doors, and usually a smaller door on each side, for the deacons. Second, the order of it. To the right of the central doors, as you face it, is Christ. To the left, his mother, holding him. Next to them often stand John the Baptist and the saint the church is named for, and in larger churches, rows above them: the great feasts, the apostles, the prophets. The whole story of salvation, hung on one screen. Third, why paint God at all. Paul writes of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God." The Greek word for image there is eikon, icon. Because God became flesh and could be seen, Catholics and Orthodox alike hold that he can be painted. The Second Council of Nicaea taught that the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. Nobody here is praying to wood. Fourth, a window, not a wall. It looks like a barrier, and people sometimes take it for one. But the faces on it are the ones the letter to the Hebrews calls "so great a cloud of witnesses." They're not keeping you out. They're showing you who's already inside, and when the doors open, the Church can see straight through to the altar. Read this way, the screen says no one walks into prayer alone. The room is full before anyone gets there.
screen: `BETWEEN THE NAVE AND THE ALTAR.` · `CHRIST ON THE RIGHT, HIS MOTHER ON THE LEFT.` · `THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.` · `A WINDOW, NOT A WALL.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an icon wall, or one icon. Settle, and breathe. If you can, bring up a photograph of an iconostasis, or any icon you have at home. Don't study it. Pick one face and stay with it. Notice the eyes, how they look straight out, not off to the side. Let yourself be looked at for a minute. If you pray, you can use an old prayer of the East, slowly, on the breath: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. If you don't, simply stay with the face, and notice what it's like to be seen. The bell holds the time.
Iconostasis. The screen of icons between the nave and the altar, with doors in the middle: a cloud of witnesses, and a window onto the altar. Today's word.
Your line: the icon screen. Today, when you walk into a room, remember the faces on the screen, and act as if the room is fuller than it looks. Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: In Byzantine churches, Catholic and Orthodox, the iconostasis separates the nave from the sanctuary; people venerate its icons with a bow, the sign of the cross, a kiss or a candle, and the doors open at set moments of the liturgy.

notes: Layout described as the usual pattern (Christ to the right of the Royal Doors, the Theotokos to the left; John the Baptist and the patron 'often'; tiers 'in larger churches'). Arrangements vary; confirm.
'The Greek word for image there is eikon' (Colossians 1:15, εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου): a word in the text, not an etymology. Confirm.
Second Council of Nicaea paraphrased: honor given to an image passes to its prototype (CCC 2132 quotes Basil via Nicaea II). Confirm.
The Jesus Prayer ('Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me') is offered as 'an old prayer of the East', in a common English form, without quotation marks or a cited translation.
'A window, not a wall' is a common way of describing the iconostasis, not quoted from a source.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Colossians 1:15 and the phrase in Hebrews 12:1.

Editor pass: fixed 'Christians in the East, and Catholics with them', which set Eastern Christians apart from Catholics in a week on Eastern Catholics; replaced the 'On an ordinary day... you never walk into prayer alone' line (stock opener, told the listener what is true for them).
